Women Fight Back

By: Kate Barry | Paid

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Enough is enough - the country rises up against gender-based violence after the killing of UCT student Nene.

Unique Selling Point:
We join the protest marches to Parliament demanding action against the perpetrators of GBV, and stricter punishment .

Summary:
We speak to the family of victims of the spate of killings of women and children in the Western Cape. We also highlight the formation of a new Facebook group called SA Women Fight Back, which has captured over 150 000 members in just one month.

Script: SA WOMEN FIGHT BACK

V/O: Meghan Cremer, Sadiqah Newman, Uyinene Mwretyana, Leighandre Jegels, Lynette Volschenk, Jesse Hess, Ayakha Jiyane and her siblings. These are just a few of the women and children who were killed around Women’s month. Sfx: “Enough is enough!”

Link: As South Africa counts the dead, thousands of women and schoolchildren are mobilizing around the country against the scourge of rape and murder. Saying enough is enough! Sfx: Crowd: “Enough is enough!”

V/O: Thursday morning saw an unprecedented gathering of thousands of citizens outside the Houses of Parliament. This was the culmination of weeks of growing outrage, and an impassioned plea for change.

Sfx: “Today we are saying enough is enough! These are our vaginas. We are not going to be raped. Not today, not again!”

V/O: Earlier in the week, the mood had been more somber at this memorial service. Link: On Monday the country learned with shock about the brutal rape and killing of 19-year old UCT student Uyinene Mwretyana. The University has declared today a day of mourning, and students have gathered in large numbers in honour of Uyinene and all the other fallen angels. Student: Something is broken. Something is very, very broken.

V/O: Nene, as she was affectionately known, had been missing since the 29th of August. Her body was found in Khayelithsa last Monday, after a 42-year-old postal worker confessed to bludgeoning her with a scale.

Voxpops: It’s terrifying, and it’s also heartbreaking because she was especially instructed by this man to come back and we put our trust into city officials. When she died, we, we died with her.
Link: Right next door to the Claremont Police Station is the Clareinch Post Office where Uyinene was raped and savagely beaten to death. At a Post Office, next to a Police Station.

V/O: While we were filming women, men and children arrived in a steady stream to pay their own tributes to the 19-year old Nene. Her murder has been the tipping point, but this heartbreak is unbearably familiar to mothers like Na-deema Newman. Nadeema: When the first gunshot rang out…
Masa: You heard it? Nadeema: Yes, it was almost like it was in my yard. This gentleman come running and he said to my husband “Uncle Yassien, your daughter is lying in the street. They just shot her.”

V/O: 26-year-old mother-of-two, Sadiqah Newman, was on her way to buy electricity when she was gunned down on the streets of Manenberg. It was the day before Women’s Day. She was 8-months pregnant. Nadeema: I came there, I took her hand and I put it in my hand and I start praying. And I asked Sadiqah, please fight for your life, Sadiqah veg! And I put my hand on her tummy and it was just, like a contraction that I felt inside her, like the baby is making herself stiff. And I didn’t feel it anymore, and when I looked down it was like water running down her. Ek kan nie!

V/O: Sadiqah was shot 8 times. Four suspects were arrested and charged with her murder. Nadeema: They’re going to appear in court on the 10th, and that will be next Tuesday. But I don’t want them to come out because they behave like animals, they have to be locked up in cages. Because why? What’s the use of killing somebody, get bail, walking outside and doing it to somebody else’s child again?

V/O: On the day that Sadiqah was murdered, police found the body of 30-year old Meghan Cremer. Meghan had been missing from her home in Philippi since the 3rd of August. A few days later three men were arrested in possession of her stolen car. Two of the suspects were out on bail at the time of her murder. Bronwyn: The day Meghan Cremer’s body was found I was on my lunch break and I was angry. I was emotional. I think for most South African women it was a sad day.

V/O: Bronwyn Litkie is the founder of a Facebook group called SA Women Fight Back. Bronwyn: And I sat on my lunch break and I started a group and I invited all of my friends. And by Saturday we had that was the Thursday. By Saturday we had 5000 members.

V/O: They started a no-bail petition which was delivered to the Athlone Magistrates Court with 60 000 signatures.

Jodie: It touched home because I am from Knysna. From the very town that Meghan was brought up and she was really known as a very sweet, gentle, soft soul. V/O: Jodie Polley, is the Project Manager for SA Women Fight Back, which is growing exponentially. Jodie: Every single province, every town, every village is becoming part of our initiative. Parliament: Our people are terrified. 70 000 women in one week joins a movement to say enough!

V/O: The group is for women only. They drive no-bail petitions, support families in court, and have staged silent vigils nationwide. The Facebook page also provides a safe platform for women to share their own stories of abuse and rape. In just one month, the group has attracted over a hundred and fifty thousand members.

Tassi: I think women are desperate. I think women are tired of being fearful in their own homes, of getting out of their cars, of being in shopping centres and worrying, are they going to get home safely? V/O: Like all the group administrators Tassi Carelse has a fulltime job and volunteers her time. Tassi: We have created a criminal database which is gender, which is focused on murders of women, rapes, domestic violence and we are actually starting to record those statistics, which are completely separate from government statistics.

Masa: Is this something you would share with the public or with this group? Tassi: Eventually we will allow the public to pull stats from the database, but this will all be to obviously you know to take to government at some point and actually show what the severity is of these crimes. V/O: Among the first names to appear on that database will no doubt be the men who killed Meghan, Sadiqah and Uyinene. But the residents of Khayalitsha already know the identity of Nene’s killer and set fire to his home on Tuesday night. The Fire and Rescue services were prevented from extinguishing the flames.

Link: Uyinene’s murder has touched the nation and sparked the protests. But the scourge of gender-based violence has been with us for decades. The difference now is there is social media, and women are united and speaking out like never before.

V/O: The day before the big protest march, UCT students picketed outside Parliament. They were met by a delegation of ministers, who seemed to have misjudged the crowd’s anger and the magnitude of the moment. Student: The conversation is over! Sisulu: Why we are here we are going to be there with you. We want to stand with you. No, no, no, no. Student: You have to understand the fact that…we are feeling pain. And why does our government come when things have already happened? Why does it have to happen before you guys address us?

V/O The students then made their way across town and demanded to see the President.

Link: The World Economic Forum is meeting in Cape Town this week. Protestors gathered outside the Cape Town Convention Centre with a message for Pres Cyril Ramaphosa. Ironically, women and schoolchildren who were protesting against violence, were met with violence.

V/O: Protecting the politicians and visiting dignitaries, the police attacked the crowd using stun guns and water cannons. The next day, the throngs of protestors refused to sing the national anthem, calling instead for decisive leadership. Finally, the President stepped up. Cyril: We are going to be addressing the issue of the harsher penalties, so that the men who rape women, and kill women must stay in jail for life.

V/O: Other proposed measures include no bail for men who rape and murder women. but for grieving families, this offers little comfort. Nadeema: The nation must stand behind them, then we must think the President is grieving with the people. If you didn’t lose a child like that, you will never know another parent’s pain. Graca: What has happened? Where did we fail?

V/O: It was UCT Chancellor, former First Lady Graca Machel, who struck the right chord. Graca: This is really a deeply-rooted crisis of our family structures; how we nurture, we educate our children to love and respect one another. This is your country. This is your society. You have to become agents of making this society healthy. You have the power to make it. Take responsibility.
